# Introduction

Hierarchical data is surprisingly common, and are commonly represented in `<svg aria-hidden="true" role="img" viewBox="0 0 581 512" style="height:1em;width:1.13em;vertical-align:-0.125em;margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto;font-size:inherit;fill:currentColor;overflow:visible;position:relative;"><path d="M581 226.6C581 119.1 450.9 32 290.5 32S0 119.1 0 226.6C0 322.4 103.3 402 239.4 418.1V480h99.1v-61.5c24.3-2.7 47.6-7.4 69.4-13.9L448 480h112l-67.4-113.7c54.5-35.4 88.4-84.9 88.4-139.7zm-466.8 14.5c0-73.5 98.9-133 220.8-133s211.9 40.7 211.9 133c0 50.1-26.5 85-70.3 106.4-2.4-1.6-4.7-2.9-6.4-3.7-10.2-5.2-27.8-10.5-27.8-10.5s86.6-6.4 86.6-92.7-90.6-87.9-90.6-87.9h-199V361c-74.1-21.5-125.2-67.1-125.2-119.9zm225.1 38.3v-55.6c57.8 0 87.8-6.8 87.8 27.3 0 36.5-38.2 28.3-87.8 28.3zm-.9 72.5H365c10.8 0 18.9 11.7 24 19.2-16.1 1.9-33 2.8-50.6 2.9v-22.1z"/></svg>`{=html} by nested lists.

Broadcasted operations can be performed over dimensions, but not through nesting or hierarchies.  
Therefore, it is useful to be able to cast nested lists into dimensional lists.  
The 'broadcast' package provides the [cast_hier2dim()](/man/cast_hier2dim.qmd) to cast a nested list into a dimensional list (AKA a recursive array).

Casting between nested and dimensional lists is not only useful for broadcasting, however.  
Casting nested lists to dimensional lists has its own merits, as dimensional lists have some advantages over nested lists beside the broadcasting, such as the following:

 - Performing sub-set operations on **multiple** recursive subsets (using the `[[` and `[[<-` operators) requires a (potentially slow) loop, whereas multi-dimensional subsets (using operator forms like `[..., ...]` and `[..., ...]<-`) are vectorized and generally much faster.
 - Re-organizing dimensions of a recursive array is generally much easier, faster, and more straight-forward than re-organizing hierarchies of a nested list.
 
 
This Vignette gives an overview of the functions 'broadcast' provides to cast between nested and dimensional lists.

 


# Cast Hierarchical List to Dimensional List

## Introduction

The [cast_hier2dim()](/man/cast_hier2dim.qmd) function casts a nested list into a dimensional list.  
This section gently introduces the properties of this function through a series of examples, where each subsequent example builds on the previous one.  
Familiarity with nested lists and dimensional lists (i.e. arrays of type `list`) is essential to follow these examples.

 

## Example 1: Basics

For a first example, consider the following list:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- list(
  group1 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    ),
    class2 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    )
  ),
  group2 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    ),
    class2 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    )
  )
)

```
:::



Before actually casting `x` into a dimensional list, one may want to know what the dimensions will become when casted as a dimensional list;  
The [hier2dim()](/man/hier2dim.qmd) function shows you that:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hier2dim(x)
#>       
#> 3 2 2
```
:::


It returns the dimensions `c(3, 2, 2)`.  

Let's now cast `x` as a dimensional list:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x2 <- cast_hier2dim(x) # actually cast nested list into dimensional list
print(x2)
#> , , 1
#> 
#>      [,1]         [,2]        
#> [1,] numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> [2,] numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> [3,] character,10 character,10
#> 
#> , , 2
#> 
#>      [,1]         [,2]        
#> [1,] numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> [2,] numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> [3,] character,10 character,10
```
:::


Using the default arguments, element `x[[i]][[j]][[k]]` corresponds to element `x2[k, j, i]` (for all `i`, `j`, and `k`).  
This can be changed, as will be shown in a later example.


As shown in the results above, [cast_hier2dim()](/man/cast_hier2dim.qmd) will obviously not preserve names by default.  
It is trivially easy to set the `dimnames` of `x2`, using [hiernames2dimnames()](/man/hier2dim.qmd):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dimnames(x2) <- hiernames2dimnames(x)
print(x2)
#> , , group1
#> 
#>        class1       class2      
#> height numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> weight numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> sex    character,10 character,10
#> 
#> , , group2
#> 
#>        class1       class2      
#> height numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> weight numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> sex    character,10 character,10
```
:::


There, the names are now correct.

As shown above, `<svg aria-hidden="true" role="img" viewBox="0 0 581 512" style="height:1em;width:1.13em;vertical-align:-0.125em;margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto;font-size:inherit;fill:currentColor;overflow:visible;position:relative;"><path d="M581 226.6C581 119.1 450.9 32 290.5 32S0 119.1 0 226.6C0 322.4 103.3 402 239.4 418.1V480h99.1v-61.5c24.3-2.7 47.6-7.4 69.4-13.9L448 480h112l-67.4-113.7c54.5-35.4 88.4-84.9 88.4-139.7zm-466.8 14.5c0-73.5 98.9-133 220.8-133s211.9 40.7 211.9 133c0 50.1-26.5 85-70.3 106.4-2.4-1.6-4.7-2.9-6.4-3.7-10.2-5.2-27.8-10.5-27.8-10.5s86.6-6.4 86.6-92.7-90.6-87.9-90.6-87.9h-199V361c-74.1-21.5-125.2-67.1-125.2-119.9zm225.1 38.3v-55.6c57.8 0 87.8-6.8 87.8 27.3 0 36.5-38.2 28.3-87.8 28.3zm-.9 72.5H365c10.8 0 18.9 11.7 24 19.2-16.1 1.9-33 2.8-50.6 2.9v-22.1z"/></svg>`{=html} will display a dimensional list more compactly than a nested list.  
Depending on the situation this may be either be desirable or undesirable.  

One can print `x2` less compactly without much effort by flattening it, using the [cast_dim2flat()](/man/cast_dim2flat.qmd) function.  
We only need to see a portion of the list in detail, so let's look at class1 from group 1 in the flattened form:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cast_dim2flat(x2[, 1, "group1", drop = FALSE])
#> $`['height', 'class1', 'group1']`
#>  [1] 170.1031 169.0504 169.6302 169.5441 170.3542 170.3423 170.5498 171.2452
#>  [9] 168.5911 168.1512
#> 
#> $`['weight', 'class1', 'group1']`
#>  [1] 79.65874 79.95531 79.14966 78.61718 81.23532 79.68988 81.95510 79.80071
#>  [9] 79.84755 79.72189
#> 
#> $`['sex', 'class1', 'group1']`
#>  [1] "M" "M" NA  "F" "M" "M" "M" NA  NA  NA
```
:::


 

Dimensional lists can be easier to work with than hierarchical lists.  
Consider, for example, printing the height of the first class of every group in a list - let's compare how to do this in a nested list vs a dimensional list.

With a nested list, doing this takes a slow, messy for-loop:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

for(i in seq_along(x)) {
  print(names(x)[i])
  x[[i]][[1]][["height"]] |> print() # slow for-loop, messy code
}
#> [1] "group1"
#>  [1] 170.1031 169.0504 169.6302 169.5441 170.3542 170.3423 170.5498 171.2452
#>  [9] 168.5911 168.1512
#> [1] "group2"
#>  [1] 170.6263 169.0713 170.8540 171.1277 170.4505 170.8758 169.3307 171.1618
#>  [9] 170.0518 171.2397
```
:::


With a dimensional list, the very same thing can be done with sleek, vectorized code; no messy loop needed:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

x2["height", 1L, ] |> print()
#> $group1
#>  [1] 170.1031 169.0504 169.6302 169.5441 170.3542 170.3423 170.5498 171.2452
#>  [9] 168.5911 168.1512
#> 
#> $group2
#>  [1] 170.6263 169.0713 170.8540 171.1277 170.4505 170.8758 169.3307 171.1618
#>  [9] 170.0518 171.2397

x2["height", 1L, , drop = FALSE] |> cast_dim2flat() # same but more informative
#> $`['height', 'class1', 'group1']`
#>  [1] 170.1031 169.0504 169.6302 169.5441 170.3542 170.3423 170.5498 171.2452
#>  [9] 168.5911 168.1512
#> 
#> $`['height', 'class1', 'group2']`
#>  [1] 170.6263 169.0713 170.8540 171.1277 170.4505 170.8758 169.3307 171.1618
#>  [9] 170.0518 171.2397
```
:::


It is also easier to re-arrange dimensions - for example using `aperm()` - than it is to re-arrange hierarchies.

 

## Example 2: Cast from outside to inside


In Example 1, the default arguments were used for [cast_hier2dim()](/man/cast_hier2dim.qmd).  
One of these arguments is `in2out`, which defaults to `TRUE`.

Consider a nested list `x` with a depth of 3, and a dimensional list `X2` with 3 dimensions, where the relationship between `x` and `x2` can be expressed as `x2 <- cast_hier2dim(x, ...)`.  
Given this, the following can be stated about `in2out`:

 - If `in2out = TRUE`, which is the default and used in Example 1, element `x[[i]][[j]][[k]]` corresponds to element `x2[k, j, i]` (for all `i`, `j`, and `k`).  
 - If `in2out = FALSE`, element `x[[i]][[j]][[k]]` corresponds to element `x2[i, j, k]` (for all `i`, `j`, and `k`).  

The default of `in2out = TRUE` was chosen, because elements in subsequent rows are close to each other, while elements in subsequent layers (third dimension) are generally not close to each other, and the default of `in2out = TRUE` attempts to retain that behaviour.

For this example, the same list will be used as in Example 1:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- list(
  group1 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    ),
    class2 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    )
  ),
  group2 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    ),
    class2 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    )
  )
)

```
:::



Let's once again cast this list to a dimensional list, but this time use `in2out = FALSE`:



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hier2dim(x, in2out = FALSE) # check once again the dimensions
#>       
#> 2 2 3
x2 <- cast_hier2dim(x, in2out = FALSE, direction.names = 1)
print(x2)
#> , , height
#> 
#>        class1     class2    
#> group1 numeric,10 numeric,10
#> group2 numeric,10 numeric,10
#> 
#> , , weight
#> 
#>        class1     class2    
#> group1 numeric,10 numeric,10
#> group2 numeric,10 numeric,10
#> 
#> , , sex
#> 
#>        class1       class2      
#> group1 character,10 character,10
#> group2 character,10 character,10
```
:::


`x2` is the casted list.
Since `in2out = FALSE`, element `x[[i]][[j]][[k]]` corresponds to element `x2[i, j, k]` (for all `i`, `j`, and `k`).  
The argument `direction.names = 1` was specified, which intelligently tries to deduce good `dimnames` for the result. So we don't have to set the dimension names via [hiernames2dimnames()](/man/hier2dim.qmd).

One can print `x2` less compactly without much effort by flattening it, again using the [cast_dim2flat()](/man/cast_dim2flat.qmd) function.  
We only need to see a portion of the list in detail, so let's look at class1 from group 1 in the flattened form:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cast_dim2flat(x2["group1", 1, , drop = FALSE])
#> $`['group1', 'class1', 'height']`
#>  [1] 168.4060 170.6462 170.1314 169.9412 169.1094 170.4804 170.0524 170.7594
#>  [9] 170.9704 168.2932
#> 
#> $`['group1', 'class1', 'weight']`
#>  [1] 79.18250 78.83340 77.31841 78.89133 77.79655 81.72484 81.37617 80.73441
#>  [9] 79.22681 79.88658
#> 
#> $`['group1', 'class1', 'sex']`
#>  [1] "M" "F" "M" "M" "F" "F" "M" "F" NA  "M"
```
:::


 



## Example 3: Padding

For Example 3, we take the same list as before, but remove `x$group1$class2`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- list(
  group1 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    )
  ),
  group2 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    ),
    class2 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    )
  )
)

```
:::


Let's first check what dimensions it will get when casted using [hier2dim()](/man/hier2dim.qmd):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hier2dim(x)
#>         padding         
#>       3       2       2
```
:::


The dimensions are the same as in Example 1: `c(3, 2, 2)`.  
But notice the **names** of the output are different: the second element has the name "padding"; this indicates that some columns won't have enough elements to completely fill the column, and so additional elements will be added as padding.

So let's cast this list as dimensional:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x2 <- cast_hier2dim(x, direction.names = 1)
print(x2)
#> , , group1
#> 
#>        class1       class2
#> height numeric,10   NULL  
#> weight numeric,10   NULL  
#> sex    character,10 NULL  
#> 
#> , , group2
#> 
#>        class1       class2      
#> height numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> weight numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> sex    character,10 character,10
```
:::


Subset `x2[, 2, 1]` is filled with `NULL`; this is the place where `x$group1$class2` was in Example 1, but since it's not there, we need to fill **something**.

Sometimes, a different value than `NULL` is desired for padding.  
So let's replace the padding value with something **really** obvious, using the `padding` argument:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x2 <- cast_hier2dim(x, padding = list(~ "this is padding!"), direction.names = 1)
print(x2)
#> , , group1
#> 
#>        class1       class2             
#> height numeric,10   ~"this is padding!"
#> weight numeric,10   ~"this is padding!"
#> sex    character,10 ~"this is padding!"
#> 
#> , , group2
#> 
#>        class1       class2      
#> height numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> weight numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> sex    character,10 character,10
```
:::


Once again, one can print or present `x2` less compactly by flattening it:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cast_dim2flat(x2)
#> $`['height', 'class1', 'group1']`
#>  [1] 168.7057 168.8211 171.5277 170.4604 170.0525 171.5031 168.2246 169.2610
#>  [9] 169.5151 169.9183
#> 
#> $`['weight', 'class1', 'group1']`
#>  [1] 79.26368 79.17399 78.59286 78.67461 80.46292 80.77072 80.23913 77.91867
#>  [9] 80.51287 78.36819
#> 
#> $`['sex', 'class1', 'group1']`
#>  [1] "F" "M" "M" NA  "F" NA  "M" NA  "F" "M"
#> 
#> $`['height', 'class2', 'group1']`
#> ~"this is padding!"
#> 
#> $`['weight', 'class2', 'group1']`
#> ~"this is padding!"
#> 
#> $`['sex', 'class2', 'group1']`
#> ~"this is padding!"
#> 
#> $`['height', 'class1', 'group2']`
#>  [1] 170.1370 167.5792 170.7400 170.9203 170.6460 169.3070 169.8468 168.6760
#>  [9] 169.1183 172.2050
#> 
#> $`['weight', 'class1', 'group2']`
#>  [1] 79.16264 80.10424 78.40294 79.67733 80.58461 81.96788 80.19904 78.26069
#>  [9] 79.76902 80.57058
#> 
#> $`['sex', 'class1', 'group2']`
#>  [1] "F" "M" "F" "F" "F" NA  NA  NA  "F" "F"
#> 
#> $`['height', 'class2', 'group2']`
#>  [1] 171.3915 168.6664 170.1766 170.1464 169.8542 169.8118 170.1925 170.8921
#>  [9] 170.4990 168.5463
#> 
#> $`['weight', 'class2', 'group2']`
#>  [1] 79.68035 79.02800 77.83254 81.61916 78.54499 80.69132 78.96349 82.02469
#>  [9] 80.04604 78.99647
#> 
#> $`['sex', 'class2', 'group2']`
#>  [1] "F" "F" NA  NA  "M" NA  NA  NA  "M" NA
```
:::


 

## Example 4: Comparing `in2out` with padding

In this example, the same nested list as from the previous example is used, to demonstrate the difference between `in2out = TRUE` (which is the default), and `in2out = FALSE`.

Consider first the original list again:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

x <- list(
  group1 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    )
  ),
  group2 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    ),
    class2 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    )
  )
)

```
:::




On the left side the list is casted as dimensional using the default of `in2out = TRUE`, with proper names assigned.  
On the right side the list is casted as dimensional using `in2out = FALSE`, again with proper names assigned.  
For the sake of this example, we will set the `dimnames` manually via [hiernames2dimnames()](/man/hier2dim.qmd).

:::{layout-ncol="2"}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x2 <- cast_hier2dim(x)
dimnames(x2) <- hiernames2dimnames(x)
print(x2)
#> , , group1
#> 
#>        class1       class2
#> height numeric,10   NULL  
#> weight numeric,10   NULL  
#> sex    character,10 NULL  
#> 
#> , , group2
#> 
#>        class1       class2      
#> height numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> weight numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> sex    character,10 character,10
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x2 <- cast_hier2dim(x, in2out = FALSE)
dimnames(x2) <- hiernames2dimnames(x, in2out = FALSE)
print(x2)
#> , , height
#> 
#>        class1     class2    
#> group1 numeric,10 NULL      
#> group2 numeric,10 numeric,10
#> 
#> , , weight
#> 
#>        class1     class2    
#> group1 numeric,10 NULL      
#> group2 numeric,10 numeric,10
#> 
#> , , sex
#> 
#>        class1       class2      
#> group1 character,10 NULL        
#> group2 character,10 character,10
```
:::


:::


 

# Cast Dimensional List to Hierarchical list

'broadcast' provides the [cast_dim2hier()](/man/cast_dim2hier.qmd):  
[cast_dim2hier()](/man/cast_dim2hier.qmd) takes a dimensional list (i.e. an array of type `list`), and casts it to a nested list.

Consider the following recursive array as an example:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

x <- array(c(as.list(1:11), ~hello, as.list(month.abb)), c(4:2))
dimnames(x) <- list(
  letters[1:4],
  LETTERS[1:3],
  c("group1", "group2")
)
print(x)
#> , , group1
#> 
#>   A B C     
#> a 1 5 9     
#> b 2 6 10    
#> c 3 7 11    
#> d 4 8 ~hello
#> 
#> , , group2
#> 
#>   A     B     C    
#> a "Jan" "May" "Sep"
#> b "Feb" "Jun" "Oct"
#> c "Mar" "Jul" "Nov"
#> d "Apr" "Aug" "Dec"
```
:::



Like [cast_hier2dim()](/man/cast_hier2dim.qmd) also has the `in2out` argument, which (again) defaults to `TRUE`.  
Let's cast the above dimensional list to a nested list, and compare the results when using `in2out = TRUE` (on the left) versus `in2out = FALSE` (on the right):


:::{layout-ncol="2"}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

x2 <- cast_dim2hier(
  x, distr.names = TRUE
)
lobstr::tree(x2)
#> <list>
#> ├─group1: <list>
#> │ ├─A: <list>
#> │ │ ├─a: 1
#> │ │ ├─b: 2
#> │ │ ├─c: 3
#> │ │ └─d: 4
#> │ ├─B: <list>
#> │ │ ├─a: 5
#> │ │ ├─b: 6
#> │ │ ├─c: 7
#> │ │ └─d: 8
#> │ └─C: <list>
#> │   ├─a: 9
#> │   ├─b: 10
#> │   ├─c: 11
#> │   └─d: S3<formula> ~hello
#> └─group2: <list>
#>   ├─A: <list>
#>   │ ├─a: "Jan"
#>   │ ├─b: "Feb"
#>   │ ├─c: "Mar"
#>   │ └─d: "Apr"
#>   ├─B: <list>
#>   │ ├─a: "May"
#>   │ ├─b: "Jun"
#>   │ ├─c: "Jul"
#>   │ └─d: "Aug"
#>   └─C: <list>
#>     ├─a: "Sep"
#>     ├─b: "Oct"
#>     ├─c: "Nov"
#>     └─d: "Dec"
```
:::




::: {.cell}

# Simple Data Wrangling Example: Turning list inside out

The cast functions can be used to turn a list inside out.

Let's start with the following list:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- list(
  group1 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(5, 170) |> as.integer(),
      weight = rnorm(5, 80)  |> as.integer(),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 5, TRUE)
    ),
    class2 = list(
      height = rnorm(5, 170)  |> as.integer(),
      weight = rnorm(5, 80) |> as.integer(),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 5, TRUE)
    )
  ),
  group2 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(5, 170) |> as.integer(),
      weight = rnorm(5, 80) |> as.integer(),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 5, TRUE)
    ),
    class2 = list(
      height = rnorm(5, 170) |> as.integer(),
      weight = rnorm(5, 80) |> as.integer(),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 5, TRUE)
    )
  )
)
```
:::



Turning this list inside out means manipulating this list such that height, weight and sex become the surface-level elements and the groups become the deepest levels.

This can be done fast & easy with 'broadcast', by casting the nested list to dimensional with `in2out = TRUE`, and then casting the dimensional list back to nested using `in2out = FALSE`.

 

First, cast nested list to dimensional list:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x2 <- cast_hier2dim(x, direction.names = 1)
print(x2)
#> , , group1
#> 
#>        class1      class2     
#> height integer,5   integer,5  
#> weight integer,5   integer,5  
#> sex    character,5 character,5
#> 
#> , , group2
#> 
#>        class1      class2     
#> height integer,5   integer,5  
#> weight integer,5   integer,5  
#> sex    character,5 character,5
```
:::


The default value for `in2out` is `TRUE`, so we don't have to specify it here.  
The `direction.names` argument in [cast_hier2dim()](/man/cast_hier2dim.qmd) will construct dimensional names for you, so you don't have to set them manually using [hiernames2dimnames()](/man/hier2dim.qmd).  


Second, cast the newly created dimensional list back to a nested list, but this time use `in2out = FALSE`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}


x3 <- cast_dim2hier(x2, in2out = FALSE, distr.names = TRUE)
lobstr::tree(x3)
#> <list>
#> ├─height: <list>
#> │ ├─class1: <list>
#> │ │ ├─group1<int [5]>: 169, 169, 170, 169, 168
#> │ │ └─group2<int [5]>: 171, 169, 170, 169, 171
#> │ └─class2: <list>
#> │   ├─group1<int [5]>: 170, 169, 171, 171, 169
#> │   └─group2<int [5]>: 169, 171, 169, 168, 172
#> ├─weight: <list>
#> │ ├─class1: <list>
#> │ │ ├─group1<int [5]>: 80, 78, 80, 79, 79
#> │ │ └─group2<int [5]>: 80, 80, 79, 80, 81
#> │ └─class2: <list>
#> │   ├─group1<int [5]>: 80, 80, 80, 79, 80
#> │   └─group2<int [5]>: 79, 80, 79, 79, 81
#> └─sex: <list>
#>   ├─class1: <list>
#>   │ ├─group1<chr [5]>: "NA", "M", "M", "M", "F"
#>   │ └─group2<chr [5]>: "F", "F", "F", "F", "M"
#>   └─class2: <list>
#>     ├─group1<chr [5]>: "M", "F", "F", "NA", "M"
#>     └─group2<chr [5]>: "M", "M", "NA", "M", "NA"
```
:::


We use `lobstr::tree()` to print the results more compactly;  
as shown, the original nested list has now successfully been turned inside-out, with great ease.
